Delirium: Tell It From Dementia and Psychosis, Then Find the Cause

Did attention fail over hours to days, and which drug or illness caused it?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line

Act first on delirium tremens: sweating, tremor, fever and a fast pulse, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink. Give an intravenous (IV) benzodiazepine now; it can be fatal.

Delirium: attention and awareness fail over a short time (usually hours to days) and tend to fluctuate, with one more cognitive change and a cause (criteria below). Dementia starts slowly, with attention spared until it is severe.

Review every drug first: anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines are common causes, and meperidine is one of the most deliriogenic opioids.

Stop the drug, treat the cause, reorient the patient and protect sleep.

Antipsychotics are not shown to shorten delirium; give one only for severe agitation that threatens safety.

Benzodiazepines treat alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal delirium; in every other delirium, avoid them.

Diagnosis
Diagnostic criteria A – attention and awareness disturbed · B – develops over a short time (usually hours to a few days), a change from baseline, and tends to fluctuate during the day · C – one more cognitive disturbance: memory, disorientation, language, visuospatial ability or perception · D – not better explained by a preexisting, established or evolving neurocognitive disorder, and not in severely reduced arousal such as coma · E – evidence of a cause: medical condition, substance intoxication or withdrawal, medication, toxin, or several · Against dementia and psychosis – timing chart
Management and treatment
Management ladder
TierInterventionEscalate when
Every patientTreat the cause; stop deliriogenic drugs; reorient; glasses and hearing aids; protect sleep; mobilizeBehavior puts the patient or others at risk
Severe agitationLow-dose antipsychotic (haloperidol, quetiapine or risperidone); baseline ECG for the QTc (rate-corrected interval)Top rung: adjust the dose daily; stop as soon as clinically feasible
By situation Alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal – IV benzodiazepine, the drug of choice; in alcohol withdrawal, no haloperidol at first · Any other cause – avoid benzodiazepines: more confusion and sedation · Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia – an atypical antipsychotic preferred · Restraint to prevent harm – trained staff; release at least every 2 hours; stop as soon as possible
Prevention and course Beers criteria – avoid meperidine in older adults; with or at high risk of delirium, also avoid anticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, corticosteroids, histamine-2 receptor antagonists, zolpidem-type hypnotics and opioids, except in listed situations · Course – usually reversible, but deficits often take weeks or months to clear; decline, institutionalization and death stay more likely for up to 2 years
Practice
  1. 72-year-old man 2 days after hip replacement since last night sees children in his room says staff stole his wallet calm mornings, agitated evenings No psychiatric history vital signs normal · fails days of the week backward · oriented to person only → Delirium → acute, fluctuating inattention with visual hallucinations and disorientation after surgery is delirium
  2. 78-year-old woman, 2 years of worsening forgetfulness repeats questions; misses bills lost driving a familiar route no day-to-day fluctuation alert · days backward correct · 0 of 3 words recalled · disoriented to date only · afebrile; vitals, blood count, chemistry, thyroid normal → Major neurocognitive disorder → slow onset over years, memory lost first, attention spared: dementia, not delirium
  3. 84-year-old woman, pneumonia, hospital day 3 drowsy; one-word answers cannot count backward from 20 son: sharp last week; is she depressed? No history of depression oxygen saturation 93% on 2 L/min · other vital signs normal · oriented to person only → Hypoactive delirium → somnolent and inattentive with an acute change from last week: hypoactive delirium, often mistaken for depression
  4. 81-year-old woman in the hospital for cellulitis given diphenhydramine for sleep last evening, her first dose overnight: confused, picks at the air T 37.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 136/80 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Anticholinergic effect → first-generation antihistamines are highly anticholinergic, a Beers delirium class
  5. 86-year-old woman from a nursing home with 1 day of confusion that comes and goes at baseline oriented; walks with a cane no new medications Neurologic examination nonfocal T 37.8 °C · HR 98/min · BP 124/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CBC, metabolic panel and urinalysis → look for the medical cause first; imaging is not routine without focal signs
  6. 77-year-old man taking warfarin fell at home 2 days ago now drowsy and confused, worse at night new weakness of the right arm Blood count and chemistry normal T 36.9 °C · HR 84/min · BP 164/90 · inattentive · oriented to person only → CT of the head without contrast → a focal sign after head trauma on an anticoagulant: look for a subdural hemorrhage
  7. 69-year-old man 2 days after knee replacement restless; says someone hides in the closet fluctuating meperidine every 4 hours for pain Not dangerous to himself or others vital signs normal · creatinine 2.1 mg/dL · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Replace meperidine with another analgesic → stop the deliriogenic drug; poor kidney clearance lets normeperidine accumulate; untreated pain also precipitates delirium, so give another analgesic
  8. 80-year-old man after bowel surgery yesterday pulls his IV, climbs bed rails, hits a nurse despite reorientation, daughter present Infection, pain treated; sedatives stopped; no alcohol T 37.6 °C · HR 102/min · BP 150/88 · inattentive · oriented to person only · QTc normal → Low-dose haloperidol → severe agitation that threatens safety despite nonpharmacologic care: low-dose antipsychotic after a QTc check
  9. 52-year-old man admitted 2 days ago for femur fracture now confused, sweaty and tremulous picks at insects he sees on sheets drank 10 beers a day until admission T 38.3 °C · HR 128/min · BP 168/98 · inattentive · oriented to person only → Intravenous benzodiazepine → alcohol withdrawal delirium, usually 48 to 72 hours after the last drink: benzodiazepines are the drug of choice
  10. 83-year-old woman on day 2 of ceftriaxone for a urinary tract infection restless and calling out at night; calmer by day not harming herself or others No alcohol or sedative use vital signs normal · inattentive · oriented to person and place → Lorazepam at bedtime → benzodiazepines worsen confusion and sedation outside withdrawal; keep treating the infection
  11. 79-year-old man with mild cognitive impairment admitted for an elective hip replacement tomorrow wears glasses and hearing aids Alert and attentive oriented to person, place and time · vital signs normal → Reorientation, mobilization and sleep protection → targeted nonpharmacologic prevention; antipsychotics are not shown to prevent episodes, and zolpidem is on the Beers delirium list
  12. 81-year-old woman, Alzheimer disease for 3 years baseline: knows family, dresses herself 1 day of drowsiness alternating with shouting cannot follow a conversation; dysuria T 38.4 °C · HR 104/min · BP 118/70 · inattentive · oriented to person only · urine: leukocyte esterase, nitrites → Delirium from a urinary tract infection → an acute change from her baseline with fever and dysuria is delirium, and dementia is a leading risk factor; Lewy body fluctuations usually span days to weeks within a chronic dementia and do not explain fever or dysuria
How NBME framed it: question 1

57-year-old woman; tibial fracture fixed (open reduction, internal fixation) 4 days ago now agitated; believes the nurses are experimenting on her and keep her from sleeping says the nurses are trying to poison her appears tremulous Hypertension, systemic lupus erythematosus; no psychiatric illness or substance abuse Medications: chloroquine, hydrochlorothiazide, meperidine, propranolol, thyroxine oriented to person and place, not time

Which drug most likely caused her symptoms?

Competing answers
  • Chloroquine: a daily drug she takes for lupus; but the explanation clears all four non-opioid options: none is linked to delirium or on the Beers list.
  • Hydrochlorothiazide: her antihypertensive; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Propranolol: a beta blocker that also treats tremor, and she is tremulous; but not linked to delirium in the explanation.
  • Thyroxine: tremor and agitation suggest too much thyroid hormone; but it treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Down to two: meperidine or thyroxine. Meperidine: new agitation, disorientation to time and paranoid delusions days after surgery is delirium, and she takes an opioid. The explanation names anticholinergics, opioids and benzodiazepines as common causes and calls meperidine and tramadol highly deliriogenic; no psychiatric or substance history argues against a primary psychosis or withdrawal. Thyroxine treats hypothyroidism and is not linked to delirium in the explanation.

Pairs with Psychosis in an Adult: Rule Out a Cause, Then Time It: exclude a medical cause first; acute onset over hours to days suggests one.
Transferable rule

In a new psychosis or confusion in a hospitalized or older patient, test attention and ask when it began: acute, fluctuating inattention points to delirium. Then read the medication list and stop the anticholinergic, opioid or benzodiazepine that started it.
